correctness.rationale: The Mwesigye-Truss character theorem reduces \((q+1)\)-equivalence to equality of the sets of \(q\)-characters. Monochromatic intervals have the classical threshold \(2^q-1\). For one red point, splitting at a selected blue or red point yields an induction in the two side lengths; the endpoint cases use threshold \(T_q\), while an interior red point spends one move exposing the red point and therefore leaves threshold \(T_q-1\) on each side. The claimed class count and maximal minimal length follow directly. A fresh independent character-recursion replay verified the canonical classification for \(q=1,2,3,4\), including counts \(2,11,51,227\); the general theorem rests on the induction, not the finite replay.
correctness.risk: The claim concerns exactly one distinguished red point and ordinary first-order Ehrenfeucht-Fraïssé rank.

value.rationale: One distinguished point is the first non-monochromatic colored-order family and turns a difficult general character recursion into a complete all-rank solution with sharp class count and representative length. That is a natural structural boundary case with reusable finite-model-theory content, not an arbitrary finite enumeration.
value.risk: The contribution is deliberately narrow and does not solve the general multi-red or multi-color profile.

final_claim: For finite linear orders with exactly one red point and all other points blue, the rank-\(q\) equivalence profile is exact: for \(q\ge2\), with \(T_q=2^q-1\), red-first and red-last orders are classified by a single truncation at \(T_q\), while interior-red orders are classified by the two side lengths truncated at \(T_q-1\). Hence there are exactly \(T_q^2+2\) rank-\(q\) classes, and the largest minimal representative has length \(2^{q+1}-3\); the \(q=1\) case has two classes.
limitations: Exactly one red point and all remaining points blue.
The general finite colored-linear-order classification remains much more complicated.
